Belgian Congo. A formal colonial state established in eighteen eighty-five as the personal possession of King Leopold the Second, then administered by Belgium from nineteen eight until independence in nineteen sixty. The colony encompassed the vast Congo River basin in central Africa, one of the world's richest repositories of natural resources including rubber, copper, and diamonds. It became one of Africa's most exploitative colonial regimes.

Belgian Congo originated as the Congo Free State under King Leopold's personal control, a fiefdom where forced labor and violence extracted rubber for export at enormous human cost. Estimates of deaths range from one to ten million. Belgium assumed direct control in nineteen eight, nominally ending the worst abuses, but exploitation and racial segregation remained systemic throughout the colonial period. The colony was administered with rigid paternalism and little investment in education or native political participation, leaving it profoundly unprepared for independence.

Patrice Lumumba became the first Prime Minister after independence in June nineteen sixty, symbolizing nationalist hopes. But he was assassinated within months during the Congo Crisis, plunging the country into civil war. The Congo Crisis from nineteen sixty to nineteen sixty-five drew international intervention and Cold War competition. Mobutu Sese Seko seized power and renamed the country Zaire.

Belgian Congo's chaotic decolonization set a pattern for post-colonial instability that would plague the region for decades. It remains central to understanding African independence and Cold War geopolitics.
